title: Who I am
job: Introduce yourself and state what you like
verifiedBy: Claude Fable 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: Word order is the English one — subject, verb, object — so a plain statement comes out in the order you already think in.

A verb ending already names its subject, so a neutral statement carries no subject pronoun: sono = I am, mi piace = I like. io and tu are not wrong, they are marked — they come back to draw a contrast (Io sono indiano, lei è italiana).
You give your name with mi chiamo — literally "I call myself". The little pronoun says whose name it is: mi chiamo · ti chiami · si chiama.
sono is essere, the "to be" of who you are and where you are from. The ending names the person — sono (I) · sei (you) · è (he, she, it).
After essere a role or a nationality stands bare: Sono studente, never Sono un studente. An article comes back only when something describes the noun (Sono un bravo studente).

Every noun has a gender and its article shows it: il (m) · la (f) · i (m pl) · le (f pl). Learn each noun with its article — the last letter is a hint and not a rule, since il problema ends in -a and is masculine and la mano ends in -o and is feminine.

Liking runs on piacere, "to be pleasing": the thing liked is the SUBJECT, so the verb agrees with IT and never with you — Mi piace il caffè (one thing) · Mi piacciono i libri (more than one). mi only says who is pleased, and it never changes.
Italian keeps the article where English drops it: Mi piace il caffè is "I like coffee", not "I like the coffee". A whole class of thing takes il or la.
An accent is a letter here, not decoration. è means "is"; e without it means "and", and the two are otherwise the same word on the page. caffè keeps its accent every time it is written.

words.note: chiamarsi, "to call oneself". The little pronoun says whose name it is: mi chiamo (mine) · ti chiami (yours) · si chiama (his or hers). This, and not il mio nome è, is how a name is given.
Names carry over unchanged — swap in your own.

sentences.trap: Il mio nome è Rohan is the English sentence translated word for word. It is grammatical, and nobody introduces themselves that way.
sentences.sound: ch is a hard k in Italian: mee KYAH-mo. The ch of "church" is written c before i or e, so chi can only be "kee".

variations.changed: mi → ti and a question mark: the same verb, asked instead of stated
mi → si: the same verb, a different person
swap the name — Mi chiamo itself never changes

mistake.why: No è — chiamo is already the verb. Mi chiamo Rohan is the whole sentence.

sentences.usage: First introductions, to anyone. This course speaks to one person you are on familiar terms with; the polite address, Lei, comes later.
sentences.mnemonic: chiamo = I call. Your name is what you call yourself, so mi chiamo.

sentences.glossEn: lit. "Am Indian" — the "I" is inside sono

words.note: essere — the "to be" of who you are, what you are and where you are from. The ending names the person: sono (I) · sei (you) · è (he, she, it). Italian gets one more use out of this shape: sono is also the form for loro, "they are", and from the past-tense module it is the helper that builds sono andato, "I went". The sentence around it is what tells you which.
An adjective of nationality, and it agrees with whoever it describes: indiano for a man, indiana for a woman. Italian writes nationalities with a small letter — indiano, never Indiano.

sentences.trap: English says the "I" out loud every time. Io sono indiano is not wrong, but it reads as insistence — I am Indian, whatever you are. The neutral sentence is Sono indiano.
sentences.sound: SO-no, two short round o's, and no swallowed vowel at the end: Italian has no schwa, so the last o is as clear as the first.

variations.changed: -o → -a: the adjective follows whoever is speaking, so a woman says indiana
sono → è: the ending swaps the person, and there is still no pronoun
a name can be the subject — and then è is the form the sentence needs

mistake.why: Drop the io — sono already says "I am". It comes back only when you are drawing a contrast.

sentences.usage: Saying where you are from, in the shape Italian reaches for first.
sentences.mnemonic: The -o ending on the verb is the "I": sono.

words.note: One little word for both "from" and "of": sono di Delhi (from), studente di musica (of), un chilo di riso (of). Every later use in this course is one of those two jobs.
City names mostly carry over, capital letter and all.

sentences.trap: Sono di takes a CITY. A country does not sit here the same way: Italian says Sono indiano, or reaches for another verb entirely — Vengo dall'India.
sentences.sound: di is one clean syllable, DEE — the i is the ee of "see", never the i of "dip".

variations.changed: swap the city — Sono di … is the frame
sono → è: the ending names a different person, and still no pronoun
sono takes your name too — and the city tags along after a comma

mistake.why: A country does not follow di this way. Name the city — Sono di Delhi — or name the nationality: Sono indiano.

sentences.usage: Where you are from, when the city says more than the country does.
sentences.mnemonic: di points backwards: from where you came, of what you are made.

sentences.glossEn: lit. "Am student" — there is no word for "a"

words.note: A man is uno studente, a woman una studentessa — unlike English "student", this noun changes shape for the person. Plural studenti.

sentences.trap: English needs the article — I am a student — and Italian leaves it out after essere. Sono studente is the whole sentence.
sentences.sound: stu-DEN-te, stressed in the middle, and the final -e is pronounced: three syllables, not two.

variations.changed: a woman says studentessa — the noun itself moves, not just an article
sono → è: he is the student now, and there is still no article
di links the two nouns — what you study comes after it

mistake.why: Two things at once: after essere a bare role is the everyday sentence — Sono studente — and un never stands before s + consonant anyway, where the article is uno.

sentences.usage: Saying what you do — work or study — when you meet someone.
sentences.mnemonic: Italian states the role, not a count of it: Sono studente.

words.note: piacere means "to be pleasing", so the thing liked is the subject and piace agrees with IT: one thing → piace. The little pronoun in front says who is pleased, and nothing else moves: mi piace (me) · ti piace (you) · gli piace (him). For more than one thing, S07 has mi piacciono.

The masculine singular article, and the article is what shows a noun's gender: il (m) · la (f) · i (m pl) · le (f pl). Before a vowel il and la both shrink to l' and join the noun: l'italiano. Italian also keeps the article where English drops it — mi piace il caffè is "I like coffee".
Masculine, so il caffè. The written accent is the stress — ka-FEH — and it never comes off. A noun ending in a stressed vowel does not change in the plural: due caffè.

sentences.trap: Io piaccio il caffè copies the English shape and ends up saying that you are the one doing the pleasing.
sentences.sound: Stress lands on the last syllable — ka-FEH — which is exactly what the written accent is telling you, and the double f is held audibly longer than a single one.

variations.changed: mi → ti: who is pleased changes, piace does not
mi → gli: now he is the one pleased — piace still does not move
an adjective follows the noun it describes — italiano after caffè

mistake.why: piacere runs the other way: the coffee pleases you. Mi piace il caffè.

sentences.usage: Likes of every kind — food, music, places, people.
sentences.mnemonic: Read it backwards and it clicks: to-me pleases the coffee.

words.note: The feminine singular article. Gender belongs to the noun and not to its last letter: il problema ends in -a and is masculine, la mano ends in -o and is feminine. Learn each noun with its article.
Feminine, so la musica. The stress falls three syllables back — MU-si-ca — and Italian writes an accent only on a final stressed vowel (caffè), so this one is learned with the word.

sentences.trap: It is still one thing being liked, so it is still piace — music does not go plural just because there is a lot of it.
sentences.sound: MU-si-ca. The u is the oo of "moon", cut short, and the c before i is the ch of "church".

variations.changed: add an adjective and it agrees with musica — italiana, not italiano
mi → ti: the person pleased changes, piace stays
mi → gli: his liking now — the pronoun set is mi · ti · gli, and piace stays put

mistake.why: English says "I like music" with no "the"; Italian needs the article for a whole class of thing: Mi piace la musica.

sentences.usage: Talking about what you enjoy — usually the first thing anyone asks.
sentences.mnemonic: A whole class of thing carries its article: la musica, il caffè.

words.note: The plural partner of S05's mi piace. More than one thing does the pleasing, so the verb goes plural — piacciono. The things decide, never you: only the little pronoun swaps for the person pleased — mi piacciono · ti piacciono · gli piacciono — and piacciono itself never moves.
Masculine plural. The noun's last vowel does the work and the article goes plural with it: il libro → i libri.
Masculine: il libro (one) · i libri (more than one). The plural is a vowel change on the ending — -o becomes -i — and never an added -s.

sentences.trap: English keeps "like" flat — I like a book, I like books. Italian moves the verb, because the books are its subject.
sentences.sound: LEE-bri, stressed on the first syllable, and the single r is one quick tap of the tongue — nothing like the English r.

variations.changed: one book, so piace and il come back
mi → ti: the person pleased changes, piacciono does not
mi → gli: a third person is pleased, and piacciono still agrees with the books

mistake.why: Two or more things are doing the pleasing, so the verb is plural: Mi piacciono i libri.

sentences.usage: Saying what you like when there is more than one of it.
sentences.mnemonic: Count the things, not the people: one → piace, many → piacciono.

words.note: Feminine plural: la canzone → le canzoni. Four articles in all — il · la · i · le — one for each pairing of gender and number.
Feminine: la canzone (one) · le canzoni (more than one). A noun in -e goes to -i in the plural whatever its gender, so the ending alone cannot tell you which gender it is — the article can.

sentences.trap: The article is doing work English does with nothing at all: "I like songs" is mi piacciono LE canzoni.
sentences.sound: kan-TSO-ni. The z is a "ts", pressed together as one sound, and never the buzzing z of English "zoo".

variations.changed: one song: la, and piace
mi → ti: the person pleased changes, and piacciono stays with the songs
molto goes straight after the verb

mistake.why: canzone is feminine, so its plural article is le: le canzoni.

sentences.usage: Songs, films, books — anything you like in the plural.
sentences.mnemonic: le canzoni — a feminine plural takes le, whatever the noun's own ending was.

sentences.glossEn: lit. "The Italian pleases me a lot"

words.note: a lot, and it sits right after the verb: mi piace molto l'italiano, never mi piace l'italiano molto. In front of a noun it becomes an adjective and agrees (molto caffè · molta musica); as the adverb here it never changes.

The language, and also the adjective. Before a vowel the article il shrinks to l' and is written onto the word — l'italiano, one word on the page. As an adjective it agrees with what it describes: il caffè italiano, la musica italiana. Italian writes languages and nationalities with a small letter.

sentences.trap: English hangs "a lot" on the end of the sentence. Italian presses it against the verb.
sentences.sound: The article and the noun run together as one word: li-ta-LYA-no. Nothing is dropped — the apostrophe is where the vowel of il used to be.

variations.changed: plural things → piacciono, and molto stays put
swap the thing liked; the frame holds, and before a consonant the article is il again
mi → ti: the person pleased changes, and molto stays glued to piace

mistake.why: molto belongs right after the verb: Mi piace molto l'italiano.

sentences.usage: Turning a like up a notch without reaching for a new verb.

words.note: essere for one other person or thing: he is, she is, it is. The accent is the whole word — e without it means "and" — so è is written with its accent every single time.
An adjective agrees with what it describes: il caffè è buono · la musica è buona · i libri sono buoni · le canzoni sono buone. It follows the noun when it describes one directly (un caffè buono).

sentences.trap: è with its accent is "is". Drop the accent and you have written "and": Il caffè e buono says "the coffee and good", which is not a sentence.
sentences.sound: è and e are the same letter with two different mouths: è is open, like the e in "bed"; plain e is closer, like the a in "gate" without the glide. The accent tells you which one to say. buono is BWO-no, two syllables.

variations.changed: a feminine subject pulls the adjective with it — buona
more than one → sono ("they are"), and the adjective goes plural too
italiano squeezes in after the noun it describes; buono is still what the sentence claims

mistake.why: Without its accent, e is "and". The verb is è — Il caffè è buono.

sentences.usage: Saying what you think of a thing — the shortest opinion the language has.
sentences.mnemonic: The accent leans on è because è is doing the work of a verb.
